title: Understanding how glandular fever affects the immune system and whether antiviral treatment changes the body's response to infection
official: Epstein Barr virus viral loads, memory B-cells repertoires, and immune response in people with and without a history of infectious mononucleosis
summary:
Background and study aims
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a very common virus that infects most people at some point in their lives. Many people have no symptoms, but some develop infectious mononucleosis (IM), also known as glandular fever. IM can cause symptoms such as a severe sore throat, fever, swollen glands and long-lasting tiredness. Previous research suggests that people who have had IM may be more likely to develop certain autoimmune diseases later in life, including multiple sclerosis.
This study aims to understand why some people develop IM while others do not, and how EBV affects the immune system. The researchers will compare people with IM, people with bacterial throat infections caused by streptococcal bacteria, and healthy volunteers. The study will also investigate whether a short course of the antiviral medicine famciclovir can affect the amount of EBV in the body and change the immune response in people with IM.

Who can participate?
People aged 16 to 35 years can take part if they have IM, a streptococcal throat infection, or are healthy volunteers. Participants must be able to give informed consent and meet the study eligibility criteria.

What does the study involve?
The study plans to recruit 80 participants.
Sixty participants will take part in an observational study:
1.	20 participants with IM
2.	20 participants with streptococcal throat infection
3.	20 healthy volunteers
A further 20 participants with IM will be offered treatment with famciclovir taken by mouth twice a day for 7 days.
Participants will provide blood samples, saliva samples and throat swabs when they join the study. They will then attend follow-up visits and provide further samples after 7 days, 28 days, 183 days, 365 days and 730 days. These samples will be used to measure EBV levels and to study how the immune system responds to infection over time.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may not receive any direct health benefit from taking part. However, the information collected could help researchers better understand how EBV causes IM and affects the immune system. The findings may support the development of future treatments and management strategies for EBV-related illnesses, including diseases linked to abnormal immune responses.
The study involves blood sampling, throat swabs and saliva collection, which may cause temporary discomfort. Participants receiving famciclovir may experience side effects associated with this medicine. The study team will explain the potential risks and side effects before participants decide whether to take part.

Where is the study run from?
The study is run from Barts Health NHS Trust at The Royal London Hospital in London, United Kingdom.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2027 to January 2030.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the Horne Family Foundation, United States of America.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Ben Bloom, ben.bloom@nhs.net
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age above 16 years 
2. Diagnosis of IM (Intervention and control group)
3. Diagnosis of streptococcal pharyngitis (control group)
4. Ability to provide Informed consent
5. Willingness to take a course of oral famciclovir (Intervention group)
Exclusion criteria:
1. Unable to comply with study requirements 
2. Unable to provide informed consent
3. Other pre-existing autoimmune diseases, for example, type I diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroid disease, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, etc. 
4. Unwilling to take a 7-day course of  famciclovir (Intervention group)
5. Concomitant treatment with probenicid and raloxifene (Intervention group)
6. Pregnant or breastfeeding (Intervention group)
